title: Apply procedures to manage damage control in animals and victims

lessons.title: Identifying damage-causing animals
lessons.html:
The problem of predation

Damage-causing animals are wild or feral animals that kill or injure livestock, damage crops or infrastructure, or threaten people. In South Africa, predation of sheep and goats by black-backed jackal and caracal causes large losses every year, and feral dogs, baboons, bushpigs, crows and eagles also cause damage. Effective damage control starts with knowing exactly which animal is responsible, because the wrong response wastes money, harms innocent wildlife and may be illegal.

Reading the evidence

Inspect carcasses and the scene soon after a loss, before scavengers change the evidence. Look for tracks, bite marks, bruising under the skin, feeding pattern and how many animals were affected. Skinning the neck and throat area of a carcass shows bite punctures and bleeding, which prove the animal was alive when attacked.

PredatorTypical signs
Black-backed jackalBite to the throat; often starts feeding from the flank or behind the ribs; usually one or a few animals
CaracalBite to the throat or back of the neck with claw marks on shoulders and back; may cover the carcass
Feral or domestic dogsMany animals injured and scattered; bites on legs, hindquarters and ears; little eaten
BaboonLambs or kids with the belly torn open, often the milk-filled stomach eaten
EagleTalon punctures on the back and head of small lambs

These are typical patterns, not certain rules. Animals that died of disease or exposure and were then scavenged show no bleeding at the bite sites. If unsure, ask an experienced predation management adviser, extension officer or vet.

Recording losses

Keep a predation register: date, camp, number and type of animals lost or injured, suspected predator and evidence, and photographs. Records show patterns such as losses peaking at lambing, help justify control actions to authorities and support insurance claims.

lessons.title: Preventing and controlling damage
lessons.html:
Prevention first

Non-lethal methods are usually the first and most sustainable line of defence. Combining several methods works better than relying on one.

  • Kraaling at night - bring small stock into a secure kraal or a camp close to the homestead, especially during lambing.
  • Planned lambing - lamb in small, well-fenced camps near people, so that vulnerable lambs can be watched.
  • Livestock guardian animals - properly bonded guarding dogs such as the Anatolian shepherd, or donkeys and alpacas, live with the flock and deter predators.
  • Fencing - well-maintained, predator-proof fencing with an apron at the bottom or electric strands reduces jackal entry. Check fences for holes and dig-unders often.
  • Protective collars - neck collars on lambs prevent throat bites by jackal and caracal.
  • Herders - shepherds with the flock during the day.
  • Deterrents - lights, noise devices and bells, rotated so predators do not get used to them.

Lethal control

When non-lethal measures fail, a specific damage-causing animal may have to be removed. Lethal control of wildlife is regulated by provincial nature conservation authorities and national biodiversity law, so:

  • Find out from the provincial conservation authority which methods are allowed and whether a permit is needed before acting.
  • Target only the problem animal. Methods such as unselective traps and poisons kill non-target animals like aardwolf, bat-eared fox, birds of prey and pets.
  • Never use poisons or agricultural chemicals for predator control unless the product is registered and permitted for that use. Misuse is illegal and very dangerous to people, dogs and wildlife.
  • Use only trained, authorised hunters and follow firearm laws and safe-shooting practice.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies: any trap or method must not cause unnecessary suffering, and traps must be checked often.

Working with neighbours

Predators move between farms. Coordinate prevention and control with neighbours and the local farmers' association for better results.

lessons.title: Caring for victims: injured animals and people
lessons.html:
Injured livestock

Animals that survive an attack often have deep wounds and are in shock. Act quickly and calmly.

  1. Move the injured animal to a quiet, shaded pen with water. Handle gently.
  2. Assess the injuries. Bites to the throat often damage the windpipe; deep wounds may reach the chest or abdomen.
  3. Call the vet for serious wounds. The vet will decide on cleaning, stitching, pain relief and antibiotics.
  4. Clean minor wounds with clean water and an antiseptic, and apply a wound spray with fly repellent to prevent fly strike.
  5. Check the animal daily for swelling, smell, maggots and fever.
  6. If an animal is suffering severely and cannot recover, it must be put down humanely without delay by a vet or a trained, authorised person, in line with the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  7. Record all treatments and withdrawal periods.

Rabies risk

Jackals, dogs, mongooses and other animals can carry rabies, a deadly controlled disease under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. A wild animal that is unusually tame, aggressive or attacks without reason may be rabid. Do not handle such animals or their victims with bare hands. Report suspected rabies to the state veterinarian. Keep farm dogs and cats vaccinated.

People as victims

Workers can be bitten by dogs or wild animals, or injured during control operations.

  • Make the area safe first; do not become a second victim.
  • For any animal bite or scratch: wash the wound immediately and thoroughly with soap and running water for about 15 minutes, then take the person to a clinic or hospital the same day. They may need rabies and tetanus treatment, even if the wound looks small.
  • Control severe bleeding with firm, direct pressure using a clean cloth.
  • Call emergency services for serious injuries and follow standard basic life support if the person is not breathing.
  • Report the incident to the supervisor and record it as required under the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

First aid must be learnt hands-on from an accredited first-aid training provider; this lesson does not replace that training.

Key points

  • Identify the predator from carcass evidence before acting, and keep a predation register.
  • Use non-lethal prevention first: kraaling, guardian animals, fencing, collars, herders.
  • Lethal control is regulated; check with the provincial conservation authority and target only the problem animal.
  • Treat injured livestock quickly, call the vet and euthanise humanely if recovery is impossible.
  • Wash any animal bite for about 15 minutes and send the person for medical care because of rabies risk.

quiz.question: Many sheep are found injured and scattered, with bites on the legs and hindquarters and little eaten. Which predator is most likely?
Why should you skin the neck area of a carcass during an investigation?

options.text: To see bite punctures and bleeding that show the animal was alive when attacked

quiz.question: Which is a non-lethal way to protect lambs from throat bites by jackal and caracal?

options.text: Shooting all wildlife on the farm

quiz.question: Before using lethal control on a damage-causing wild animal, what should you do?

options.text: Use any farm chemical as poison
Ask neighbours to set traps everywhere
Wait until the next lambing season
Check with the provincial conservation authority which methods are allowed and whether a permit is needed

quiz.question: A worker is bitten by a farm dog. What is the correct first step for the wound?

options.text: Cover it with a plaster and carry on working
Wash it with soap and running water for about 15 minutes, then go to a clinic
Wait to see if it becomes infected
